# The databases: GEO, SRA, ENA and friends {#sec-databases}

Several databases are involved, and papers name whichever one the authors
submitted to. Knowing what each one holds saves a lot of clicking around.

## Who holds what

| Database | Run by | Holds | You go there for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GEO** (Gene Expression Omnibus) | NCBI (USA) | Experiment descriptions, sample metadata, **processed** files (count tables, bigWigs, peaks) | The sample list and the authors' processed results |
| **SRA** (Sequence Read Archive) | NCBI (USA) | **Raw reads**, stored in NCBI's own `.sra` format | The raw data, through the SRA Toolkit |
| **ENA** (European Nucleotide Archive) | EMBL-EBI (UK) | Raw reads, also offered as ready-made **`.fastq.gz`** | The same raw data, without the SRA Toolkit |
| **DDBJ** | Japan | Raw reads | Rarely needed directly |
| **BioProject** / **BioSample** | NCBI | The project and sample records that tie everything together | Cross-referencing |
| **dbGaP** / **EGA** | NCBI / EBI | **Controlled-access** human data (patients) | Needs an approved application ([Special cases](special-cases.qmd)) |

SRA, ENA and DDBJ are the three members of the **INSDC** (International
Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration) and **mirror each other**: a run
submitted to any one appears in all three, usually within days. So an `SRR`
accession from NCBI can be downloaded from ENA, and an `ERR` from ENA can be
downloaded with the SRA Toolkit.

## How GEO and SRA fit together

When authors submit sequencing data to GEO, GEO keeps the description and
the processed files, and **passes the raw reads to SRA**. A GEO sample page
(GSM) has a link to its SRA records at the bottom.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false}}}%%
flowchart TD
  GSE["GEO Series GSE52778<br/>(the experiment)"] --> GSM1["GEO Sample GSM1275862<br/>N61311_untreated"]
  GSE --> GSM2["GEO Sample GSM1275863<br/>N61311_Dex"]
  GSE -.processed files.-> SUP["GSE52778_RAW.tar,<br/>count tables, ..."]
  GSM1 --> SRX1["SRA Experiment SRX384345<br/>(library + sequencing details)"]
  SRX1 --> SRR1["SRA Run SRR1039508<br/>(the reads)"]
  GSM2 --> SRX2["SRX384346"] --> SRR2["SRR1039509"]
```

## Processed or raw: which do you need?

Before you download terabytes, check what you need:

| You want to... | Download |
|---|---|
| Look at the authors' signal in a browser, or re-plot their result | **GEO supplementary files** (bigWigs, count tables). No toolkit needed: these are plain HTTPS links on the GSE page |
| Compare their data with yours, processed the **same** way | **Raw reads** from SRA/ENA, run through your pipeline |
| Use a newer genome build or annotation | Raw reads |
| Check their QC | Raw reads |

For comparing to your own data, raw reads processed with your own pipeline
are almost always the right choice. Differences in aligners, annotations and
normalisation between labs can be larger than the biology you want to compare.

## What's in an `.sra` file?

SRA doesn't store FASTQ. It stores each run in its own compressed,
column-based format (`.sra`). The **SRA Toolkit** converts it back to FASTQ.
SRA offers two versions of most runs:

| Format | Extension | Quality scores | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SRA Normalized** | `.sra` | The original per-base qualities | Larger |
| **SRA Lite** | `.sralite` | **Simplified**: every base gets the same quality: 30 if the read passed filter, 3 if it was rejected | About 60 % smaller |

Which one you get depends on what exists for that run and on a toolkit
setting ([Setup](setup.qmd#sra-lite-or-normalized)); some older runs exist
only in one form.
For counting genes or calling peaks, Lite is usually fine. For anything that
uses base qualities (variant calling, careful quality trimming, judging
sequencing quality with FastQC), you want Normalized. With Lite data, FastQC's
quality plot is a flat line at 30. That's a sign of the format, not a
perfect run.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. A paper says "data are available at ENA under PRJEB12345". Can you use
   `prefetch` to get them?
2. You only want to show the authors' ChIP signal next to yours in IGV. Do you
   need the SRA Toolkit?
3. Your downloaded FASTQ's quality line is `?????????...` for every read.
   Why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. Yes. The INSDC databases mirror each other, so the runs (`ERR...`) are also
   available through SRA. Or download `.fastq.gz` from ENA directly.
2. Probably not: check the GEO supplementary files for bigWigs. Only if you
   want to reprocess them identically to yours do you need the raw reads.
3. `?` is Q30 in Phred+33. You got SRA Lite data with simplified quality scores.
:::
:::
